extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in political science and the study of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: A classic expository treatment (Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion) describing principles and standards for understanding how publics form beliefs and act on them; it is addressed to analysts of public opinion and concerned citizens. The text emphasizes the role of images, stereotypes, media, and pseudo-environments in shaping behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular relationship of action, picture, and response
rubrics_metrics.description: The analyst of public opinion must begin by recognizing the triangular relationship between the scene of action, the human picture of that scene, and the human response to that picture working itself out upon the scene of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat political behavior as a double drama: interior motive (the picture in people's heads) and external behavior (acts in the real environment). Example: quarrel ostensibly about money but explained by a memory reenacted in the mind's eye. Investigate the mental image that motivates actions rather than assuming direct perception of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: People act on pseudo-environments, not the real environment
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an insertion between man and his environment of a pseudo-environment; to that pseudo-environment his behavior is a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining actions, analyze the constructed representation (pseudo-environment) that people treat as reality. Look for contradictions that arise when actions based on the pseudo-environment meet the real world (maladjustment). Example: islanders who acted on out-of-date news; Senators acted on a rumor about marines being landed without authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictures (mental images) determine effort and feeling, not outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The way in which the world is imagined determines at any particular moment what men will do — it determines their effort, their feelings, their hopes, not their accomplishments and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between beliefs that motivate behavior and the actual effects of those behaviors. Analysts should trace how particular images generate efforts and emotional responses regardless of objective outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictions and models vary in fidelity and may be legitimate tools
rubrics_metrics.description: By fictions I do not mean lies. I mean a representation of the environment which is in lesser or greater degree made by man himself. A work of fiction may have almost any degree of fidelity, and so long as the degree of fidelity can be taken into account, fiction is not misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat schemata, stereotypes, and models as analytic instruments; evaluate their fidelity and whether their simplifications are appropriate for the problem. Avoid dismissing all nonliteral representations as misinformation; instead assess how their inaccuracy affects decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for time-lags and intervals in information (temporal maladjustment)
rubrics_metrics.description: People may continue to act on an out-of-date picture of the world for an interval until new information arrives, producing maladjustment when their picture no longer corresponds to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include temporal factors when evaluating public beliefs: delays in news, slow communication, and celebratory or premature reactions can lead to costly errors. Example: communities acting on old war news; celebrations before an armistice followed by casualties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine symbolic personalities and stereotypes as drivers of mass opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men are usually known to the public only through a fictitious personality. Symbolic pictures of leaders (heroes and devils) govern behavior and feeling; public opinion often concentrates on symbolic personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how leaders are personified, how symbolic roles are constructed, and how hero-worship or demonization mobilizes sentiment. Use examples (Joffre, Wilson, the Kaiser) to show how symbolic images can encapsulate hopes or fears and influence mass action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that propaganda deliberately shapes pictures people respond to
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is the effort to alter the picture to which men respond, to substitute one social pattern for another; class consciousness and national consciousness are ways of realizing the world by changing pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing campaigns or communications, treat them as interventions aimed at reshaping pseudo-environments. Evaluate their techniques and success in forming collective images (e.g., creating class consciousness) rather than assuming persuasion operates only by conveying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate media and sources of misinformation, including deliberate deception
rubrics_metrics.description: News and rumors can intentionally or unintentionally create misleading pictures; some pictures are furnished with intent to deceive and can provoke partisan or institutional responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace provenance of reports and assess motives of information sources. Example: a man who cared nothing about the Adriatic but sought to defeat the League furnished a picture that influenced Senators; analysts should detect such deliberate framings and their political aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion usually reflects a balancing of competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In times of moderate security, symbols of public opinion bear the marks of balancing interest: check and comparison, argument, conflict, choice, hesitation, and compromise rather than perfect unanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming monolithic public views; study the array of competing symbols and interests, how they coalesce or fragment, and how factions moderate one another. Use the post-armistice breakdown of Allied Unity as an example of shifting symbolic coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize about innate human nature without comparing environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Before generalizing about innate differences of men, fix attention upon the extraordinary differences in what men know of the world. Behavior observed is response to environments (or pseudo-environments), so conclude about nature only after controlling for environmental variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comparative analysis, measure similarity of information environments before attributing behavioral differences to innate qualities. The pragmatic lesson: separate effects of knowledge/pictures from assumed biological constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study variety in knowledge across social groups as explanatory factor
rubrics_metrics.description: There are extraordinary differences in what men know of the world — classes, sections, cliques, occupations, provinces each have their own images — and these differences largely determine political behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the distribution of knowledge and images across groups (parties, classes, professions) to explain divergent actions. Do not treat populations as uniform; identify the different pseudo-environments that guide subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze feedback: images can create actions that change the real environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain conditions men respond as powerfully to fictions as to realities, and in many cases they help to create the very fictions to which they respond; actions based on images operate in the real environment and can produce consequences that confirm or contradict the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the dynamic interplay between belief and consequence: how collective action reinforces or undermines the originating image. Watch for self-fulfilling prophecies and destructive maladjustments (Herbert Spencer's 'Beautiful Theory' vs 'Brutal Facts').
